name: Wei Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. Is that okay?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yep, that's fine. I'm on days off, so I've got time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a dragline at an open-pit coal mine. A dragline is a machine the size of a block of flats that swings a bucket on cables to strip the dirt off the coal seam, and there are only four of them on our site. I'm the senior operator on my shift, I've been in the seat since I was twenty-two, and I train the operators coming up. A good day is when you're swinging and dumping in under sixty seconds a cycle and the spoil pile is neat. A bad day is a cable snap, or the dust when the wind turns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I expected. The tools get a bit better, the work stays the same. I'd probably not say anything online, maybe make a joke on the break about computers taking over the coffee machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep the seat, which is what I want. Draglines last forty years, and so can I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working, keep paying the house off, help Dad on weekends with his trucks. Maybe find a girl who doesn't mind shift work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly for Dad's trucking business. I use one to sort out his invoices and fuel logs when he gets behind. Dad drives three trucks and runs the business off a shoebox of receipts, so the AI does in ten minutes what used to take my Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself in a few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still on the dragline, maybe running the whole fleet of four. Married, hopefully. Kids eventually. Close to family.

S0.say: He'd say it's about what he expected: tools get a bit better and the work stays the same. He wouldn't post online, but might joke at break time about computers taking over the coffee machine.
S0.think: He thinks it means he keeps his seat, which is what he wants, and that draglines and he can both last forty years.
S0.do: Keeps working and paying off his house, and helps his father with the trucking business on weekends. Hopes to meet a partner who doesn't mind shift work.
S0.quote: Dad drives three trucks and runs the business off a shoebox of receipts, so the AI does in ten minutes what used to take my Sunday.
S0.fieldNote: Wei is grounded and family-centred, with a practical use for AI in his father's small trucking business. His plans are traditional: marriage, children, staying near family. The dragline gives him a sense of permanence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if a machine does it cheaper and safer, that's the market, and fair enough. But companies should look after the people who built the business. Train them, don't just bin them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a few years before they touch the draglines. They're expensive and there aren't many. But the trucks and the dozers will go first, and that's a lot of mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and learn whatever system they bring in, once I'd seen it run. I'd help Dad think about whether his trucks will be affected, because a lot of his work is hauling for the mine. And I'd put a bit more aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm all right, but it's close to home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Draglines are big and few. Do you think they'd be automated early or late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Late. They've got some automated swing control already, where the machine handles part of the cycle. It still needs me to read the ground, and the day it doesn't, I'll know before anyone in head office does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, it's always something, son, keep your head down and work. And then he'd worry about his trucks in private.

S1.say: He'd say cheaper and safer machines are the market and fair enough, but companies should train the people who built the business rather than bin them.
S1.think: He thinks draglines will be automated late because they're expensive and few, but trucks and dozers will go first, taking many friends with them.
S1.do: Keeps his job and learns the new system once he's seen it work. Helps his father think through the risk to his trucking business, which hauls for the mine, and saves a bit more.
S1.feel: Uneasy: fine himself, but it's close to home.
S1.quote: It still needs me to read the ground, and the day it doesn't, I'll know before anyone in head office does.
S1.fieldNote: Wei accepts market logic but expects companies to do right by loyal workers. His worry quickly moves from himself to his father's trucking business, which depends on the mine. He'd adopt new systems, but only after seeing them proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happened and we need to deal with it. I'd want companies to pay proper redundancy and help people get back on their feet. I don't want everybody living on benefits forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I lose the dragline and Dad loses the trucks, both in two years. I've got money and the house, but that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything big, and I'd pay off the house as fast as I could. I'd sit down with Dad and my brothers and work out how to use our savings together, maybe buying land or a small business that's harder to automate. I'd lean on family first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like hearing a cable creak just before it snaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your dad's trucking business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what hurts. Dad built that business from one truck over twenty-five years, and in two years a truck with no driver makes it worthless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to. But I'd want it tied to work or training, not just handed out. I'd go to family before government.

S2.say: He'd say it's happened and has to be dealt with, wanting companies to pay proper redundancy and help people back on their feet rather than leaving everyone on welfare forever.
S2.think: He thinks he loses the dragline and his father loses the trucks within two years, leaving him only his savings and his house.
S2.do: Stops big spending and pays off the house as fast as possible. Pools savings with his father and brothers to look at land or a small business that's harder to automate, leaning on family first.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like hearing a cable creak before it snaps.
S2.quote: Dad built that business from one truck over twenty-five years, and in two years a truck with no driver makes it worthless.
S2.fieldNote: Wei's alarm is mostly about his father's 25-year business, which would become worthless along with his own job. He'd accept government help only if tied to work or training. Family comes before the state in every plan he makes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort it properly. Companies should plan the handover and look after loyal workers. I'd say the same at the pub and in the lunch hut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to set something up with Dad and my brothers. Not enough to change careers properly, but enough to build something we own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the dragline as long as it lasts. In the first year, I'd help Dad sell two trucks while they're still worth something and put the money with mine into a small quarry or a block of land. I'd do a short course on running a business at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to stay in mining, or get out early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay as long as the money is good, then get out on my own terms. I'd rather own a little quarry with my brothers than be the last man in a big mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your younger brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn a trade with his hands, but also learn the computer side. He's nineteen. He's got more years to cover than me.

S3.say: He'd say there's time to sort it properly, with companies planning the handover and looking after loyal workers.
S3.think: He thinks five years is enough to set something up with his father and brothers, not a full career change but something they own.
S3.do: Keeps the dragline job as long as it lasts. Helps his father sell two trucks while they're worth something and pools the money into a small quarry or land, and takes a night course in running a business.
S3.quote: I'd rather own a little quarry with my brothers than be the last man in a big mine.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Wei's plan is a family-owned business built from his savings and his father's trucks. He'd stay in mining as long as the wage is good but leave on his own terms. He wants his younger brother to have both hands-on and computer skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people are sensible. Don't panic, plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get most of a good career in. Draglines will be some of the last machines to go, so I'd probably be in the seat until 2033 or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd carry on. Around year three I'd start the family business plan with Dad, and by year six I'd have the quarry or land set up. Keep saving all along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far enough away that I can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Does it feel long to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Ten years is about how long I've been working. Ten years ago I was sixteen and wanted a motorbike, so ten years can turn a whole life around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about marriage or kids in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd still want to marry and have kids. People had kids through wars and droughts. I'd just make sure we owned the house first.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty of time if people are sensible. His advice would be not to panic, and to plan instead.
S4.think: He thinks he'd get most of a good career in, since draglines will be among the last machines to go, keeping him in the seat until about 2033.
S4.do: Carries on in year one, starts the family business plan with his father around year three, and has a quarry or land set up by year six. Keeps saving throughout.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but far enough off to plan around.
S4.quote: Ten years ago I was sixteen and wanted a motorbike, so ten years can turn a whole life around.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Wei follow a sensible, step-by-step plan. He doesn't change his hopes for marriage and children, reasoning that people raised families through wars and droughts. Owning the house first remains his foundation.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes me and Dad at the same time. What would help is time, and companies having to pay proper redundancy so families can start something of their own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe pride. A dragline swing done right is a beautiful thing, and I don't know if anyone will ever see it again once the robots run them. That's what I'd miss.

headlineQuote: A dragline swing done right is a beautiful thing, and I don't know if anyone will ever see it again once the robots run them.
portrait: Wei Diaz is 27, a senior dragline operator at an open-pit coal mine who trains new operators and owns his own house. He is single, close to his parents and brothers, and uses AI now and then to sort out his father's invoices for a small three-truck trucking business. He is calm if AI fizzles, uneasy in Steady Disruption, and alarmed when AGI arrives in two years and takes both his job and his father's business at once. With five or ten years, he plans to pool family savings into a quarry or land the family owns, while staying in the dragline seat as long as it lasts.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it would take his job and his father's business at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Time, and companies required to pay proper redundancy so families can start something of their own.
